assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 1.C Ask questions that arise from initial observations of patterns in the images depicting anatomical similarities and differences of penguins that are alive today and of a fossil of a penguin from long ago.
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for
It is important that all questions posed by students be placed on the DQB regardless of whether they are open-ended or close-ended.
Make note of any close-ended questions and use navigation time throughout the unit to turn close-ended questions into open-ended ones that necessitate a need to examine additional evidence.
As you move into the discussion of ideas for future investigations and data we need, have students focus on categorizing their questions and then identifying the kinds of data and additional information that would be helpful in answering each category of questions.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students are struggling to generate questions connected to their previous observations, direct them to their sketch of a penguin from long ago, related phenomena, and other resources. If students are struggling to seek information that could inform the explanations they developed in Initial Explanations, point them to specific points and ask, What would you need to know more about to figure this out?
A DQB provides a public representation of the class’s joint mission. Students can share their questions and wonderings with one another, and the visual representation offers another modality for students to access science in the classroom. It should be centrally located in the classroom so that it can be referenced and added to throughout the unit.

What to do: If students are struggling you can allow them to work with a partner and/or use the following prompts to push them in their thinking:
What evidence would you need to support your claim?
What evidence would you need to refute the claim?
How might that piece of evidence support (or refute) your claim?
Why would that evidence convince you? What other kinds of evidence might you need?

assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 1.A Analyze and interpret data using data cards containing photos, maps, charts, measurements, and descriptive text to find patterns in penguins that are alive today.
assessments.lookListenFor: What to look and listen for: Each student should take the lead for at least one of the three ways their small group sorts the cards and co-facilitate the discussion about the patterns they notice as they do this. Students will get to work with these data sets and others multiple times over the course of the early lessons in the unit, so look for growth in fluency with this sort of data analysis in this lesson and as the unit progresses.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: Though students will have had prior experience with this element, this data set is larger and more complex. If some students find it overwhelming to look at all the cards at once, suggest that the group divide their set among them, as described above. You might also suggest a category students could begin sorting with, and then help them find other possible categories to use after that.
Share groupings, observations, and new questions that surfaced. After students have had sufficient time to sort the cards, have several groups share what they noticed, how they sorted the cards, and any new questions that came up. As students share their ideas, take note of the groupings; consider writing the groupings on the board.
Suggested prompt
Sample student response
How did you sort your cards? What connections did you discover?
We sorted based on distribution - where they usually live. We noticed that most penguins are in Antarctica, but some are in slightly warmer climates. We also noticed that all penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere.
We sorted based on penguin height. We noticed that there are clearly some very large penguins and some small penguins, but most penguins seem to be medium sized.
We sorted based on how deep the penguins can dive. We noticed that the bigger penguins can dive deeper.
What new questions came up?
(Accept all responses.)
Emphasize that we have already made some big progress in finding connections among these penguins just by looking for patterns in the different categories of data.
Examine the pattern of distribution more closely using a map. Refer to any suggestion that came up regarding patterns related to geography and say, Patterns in geographic location can be tricky to visualize without a map. Let’s discuss that one further by referencing the map of the Southern Hemisphere that’s on our data cards and then let’s discuss again some of the patterns you noticed.
Project the map on slide N and ask students about the patterns in distribution. At this point, accept all student ideas.
Suggested prompt
Sample student response
What patterns did you notice in the geographic location of different species of penguins?
All penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere.
All penguins live on or near a coast.
Some penguins lived closer to the center of the map--the South Pole--than others.
The largest penguins lived closer to the South Pole.
There was an overlap in the areas where some of the penguins lived.
Pedro was in the same place as some of the penguins of today.
What questions do you have now?
Why do the bigger penguins live further south?
Why don’t any penguins live in the Northern Hemisphere?
Are there other “Pedros” out there?
Are there fossils of other kinds of penguins?
Where would other penguin fossils be found?
Are there fossils of other kinds of animals that lived at the time of Pedro that were the predators or prey of penguins?
Summarize by saying, Just from considering geographic connections we came up with new questions. And many came from thinking about where Pedro’s fossil was found. So far, we have only looked at Pedro’s fossil, but we heard ideas and questions related to where else penguin fossils might be found. Let’s dig into that line of thinking a bit more.

Additional Lesson 2 Teacher Guidance
SUPPORTING STUDENTS IN MAKING CONNECTIONS IN ELA
CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.SL.8.1 Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions (one-on-one, in groups, and teacher-led) with diverse partners on grade 8 topics, texts, and issues, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly.
In this lesson, students collaborate with a partner to analyze data about internal and external body structures of penguins. The partners must discuss the data as they compare them, expressing their own ideas and building on their partner’s ideas. At several points in the lesson partnerships then also share their findings with the whole class.

assessments.title: Look for: Any claim is acceptable (e.g., Pedro is an an…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: Any claim is acceptable (e.g., Pedro is an an…
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look for: The questions on New Questions and Ideas for Data We Need are “Do you think Pedro could be an ancient ancestor of any of the modern penguins? Why or why not?” You will look for the following on the student handouts you collect at the end of this day:
Any claim is acceptable (e.g., Pedro is an ancestor, is not an ancestor, is related in some other way to modern penguins or other ancient penguins, and so forth).
Justification should include citing patterns in the heritable body structure data:
Pedro's entire set of known body structure variations doesn’t match any of the modern penguins.
If students say he is not related (or not an ancestor), they should discuss the amount of body structure variation that would need to match or be similar enough in order for them to be related. Ideally, students may also raise a potential problem with this logic, since it implies that you can only be related if you match on every or most heritable characteristic, but there are examples in humans or cattle (from the Muscles Unit) that they know about that refute that.
If they say he is related or might be related, they should discuss how that is possible given he has so few body structure variations in common with any modern penguins and include some kind of connection between the number of characteristics in common and relatedness (e.g., might be a distant ancestor because distant ancestors might be less like future generations than more-immediate ancestors).
assessments.whatToDo: What to do: If they don’t cite evidence based on the body structure variation data in the strips, then ask this general question on the handout: What particular patterns in the body structures that you compared led you to make this argument?

assessments.whatToDo:
Recall that Progress Tracker entries should not be scored or graded because doing so would invalidate their purpose--to be a safe space for students to process and record their thoughts honestly and without worry about evaluation. At the end of this lesson, students will complete a reflection on their Progress Tracker entry and other ideas they have built in this lesson. You can collect that reflection as a formative assessment; see the related assessment guidance callout box for 3.B at the end of day 2 of this lesson.
Transition to the next activity. Say something like, Now that you have had a chance to compare the patterns you found with your classmates’ ideas about body structures, let’s continue to explore this question of how ancient and modern penguins might be connected. Some of you wondered about where these ancient penguins were living and what their environment was like at the time, so I have some additional data about that for us to investigate.

assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 3.A Develop and use a timeline of a large data set to identify patterns in variations in body structures found in different penguins across different points in time.
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for
Placement of the following groups of penguins over the corresponding horizontal, color-coded section of their timeline
Clustering based on number of body structure similarities in the purple time period
P. gunnari and colossus together (All known body structures are in common for which values were measured.)
P. devriesi and W. tuatahi separated from P. gunnari and colossus
Clustering based on number of body structure similarities in the pink time period
different number of body structures in common between Simpson’s and Lopdell’s versus Simpson’s and Lowe’s
Clustering based on number of body structure similarities in the blue time period
Tiny rower and slender-footed together (All known body structures are in common for which values were measured.)
Pa. antarcticus near slender-footed and S. urbani and tiny rower (one structure is different between each of these) but further away from tiny rower
S. urbani further away from tiny-rower than other two (slender-footed and Pa. antarcticus)
Clustering based on number of body structure similarities in modern penguins
major clusters by number of internal body structures in common
possible minor clusters by number of external body structures or behaviors in common
assessments.whatToDo: What to do: If students simply arrange the strips in order by time and not by body structure patterns as well, emphasize that organizing by time is a good first step. Then encourage students to next look for body structure patterns both among the penguins in a given time period and in penguins across time.
assessments.description: OpenSciEd Unit 8.6 Lesson 03 — assessment opportunity from Teacher Edition.

assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for
None of the ancient penguins have all the same body structure variations in common with any modern penguins.
Ancient penguin fossils tend to have more body structure variations in common with each other the closer they are in time.
Modern penguins have more traits in common with less-ancient penguin fossils than with more-ancient ones.
The overall size of many but not all ancient penguins was larger than the largest modern penguins; the beak size and shape of many ancient penguins was longer and/or more curved than modern penguins.
Penguins living at different times experienced differences in Earth’s climate, the positions of the continents, and sea levels.
Ancient penguins lived in South America, Antarctica, and New Zealand. Depending on where the penguins lived and when they lived there, the other organisms that lived in these areas varied.
assessments.whatToDo: What to do: Since students have built towards this lesson-level performance expectation in their Progress Tracker and in Ancient Penguin Sorting Exit Ticket at two different points in the lesson, you should expect to see many of the patterns listed above. If any students neglect to mention an entire category of patterns, such as any based on shared traits or time or geography, leave a sticky note on their exit ticket for the student to respond to. Include both a noticing and a wondering on this note. In your noticing, emphasize the category of patterns that the student already noted. In your wondering, raise a question related to the category of patterns you would like them to consider further. For example, I noticed you found many patterns in how the traits of penguins compared across time. This was very interesting. I have a question. Did you find any patterns in the traits of the penguins compared to where they lived? Make sure to provide time in an upcoming class for students to respond to this feedback.

assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 4.B Develop an explanation that predicts what the variation in a chosen body structure or behavior of Galápagos penguins and king penguins looks like at different scales (between species versus between individuals within a population).
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students are struggling with differentiating the between-species and within-population variations, use the height example as a comparison and walk them through the sequence of thinking for comparing height, then ask the students to do the same for the structure they chose. Two good options to steer students toward are weight and incubation time.
The reason this distinction is important to establish now is that eventually we need to figure out that some individuals will have variations that make them more successful (at getting resources, escaping predators, attracting mates, and so forth) under certain conditions compared to other individuals in the same population with different variations.

assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 4.B Develop an explanation that predicts what the variation in a chosen body structure or behavior of Galápagos penguins and king penguins looks like at different scales (between species versus between individuals within a population).
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look for: Students should include the following ideas in their predictions:
At different scales of penguin groups (between species versus between individuals within a population of a species), the variation we are accounting for is different.
Within a population of the same species of penguin we can also look at variation within a trait (a body structure or behavior that species has)--this variation makes individuals within a population different from one another.
We look at variations of body structures or behaviors that are shared among all individuals in a species of penguin, and we look for differences in these variations of body structures or behaviors between different species of penguins.

The reason this distinction is important to establish now is that eventually we need to figure out that some individuals will have variations that make them more successful (at getting resources, escaping predators, attracting mates, and so forth) under certain conditions compared to other individuals in the same population with different variations.

assessments.title: Look for: The structures of some living things today lo…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: The structures of some living things today lo…
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 5.A.1 Analyze and interpret data from images to identify patterns of similarities and differences in modern organisms and the fossil record and use the patterns to reconstruct relationships between fossil (ancient) and extant (modern) organisms.
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for: Circulate as students work to formatively assess students’ identification and use of patterns to sort ancient and modern organisms based on their body structures. Different groups may have focused on different body structures and noticed different patterns that led to different organizations. Listen for these general ideas:
The structures of some living things today look similar to but not exactly like the most-similar-looking fossils we can find.
Sometimes, but not always, there are noticeable structural differences.
Sometimes, but not always, there are differences in overall size of the organism.
Look for students to sort and arrange their specific organism data cards based on the following body structures and variations:
horseshoe crabs: shape of shell, position of eyes, number of spines
horses: number and size of toes, shape and size of teeth
whales: presence or size of hind limbs, presence or absence of teeth, short or long skull, position of blow hole on skull
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students are struggling to identify patterns among the organisms, help them focus specifically on the structural body structures they’ve identified as important. Ask them to verbally explain or to show you visually what is similar and what is different among the organisms. Prompt them to group together things they’d describe as mostly similar and divide into separate groupings those things they’d describe as mostly different.
You may also choose to assess student understanding when students use stickers to record in their science notebooks the patterns they found after the gallery walk and discussion in the next step.

assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for: By this final un…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for: By this final un…
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 5.B.1 Respectfully provide and receive critiques about models of the similarities and differences (patterns, stability, and change) in some of the body structures of organisms observed over time and in different environments based on evidence from the fossil record.
assessments.lookListenFor: What to look and listen for: By this final unit of 8th grade, students should be very familiar with classroom norms that guide respectful conversations. Closely listening and trying to make sense of their peers’ ideas should be a well-established practice in small-group argument sharing. Though students are not yet building mechanistic explanations, they should be supporting their ideas and organizational models with patterns in the data sets that their peers shared. Students should also be posing and responding to questions to elicit additional details or to clarify the patterns in these models when there is something they don’t understand.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If you see or hear students struggling to maintain a respectful tone of voice or failing to support their critiques with ideas from the data cards, point them back to the classroom norms and other expectations you have set for productive discussions. As needed, provide sentence starters such as those from the Communicating in Scientific Ways poster from Lesson 1. You might also use sentence starters such as these: “I see …”, “I notice …”, “The reason I think my evidence supports my claim is because …”, and ”The model shows that ….”
Display slide D. Distribute to each student the appropriate set of stickers from Horse Stickers, Horseshoe Crab Stickers, or Whale Stickers. Students should use stickers of their organisms to individually record in their science notebook their revised model along with explanatory notes so they can revisit their thinking on day 2 and later in the unit. This is similar to what they did in Lesson 2.

assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for: Circulate as stu…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for: Circulate as stu…
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 5.A.2 Analyze and interpret data from images to identify patterns of similarities and differences in modern organisms and the fossil record and use the patterns to reconstruct relationships between fossil (ancient) and extant (modern) organisms.
assessments.lookListenFor: What to look and listen for: Circulate as students work to formatively assess students’ identification and use of patterns to sort ancient and modern organisms based on their body structures and location and environment or when they lived. Different groups may have noticed different patterns that led to different organizations. See the Key Ideas box for specific ideas to listen for.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students are struggling, then revisit the cards for their organism. Ask them questions such as, What do you notice is similar or different in the data between ________ and ______ organisms? Do you see any possible patterns in those similarities? What about patterns in differences on the _____ data card versus the ______ data card? Do you see that anywhere else? If needed, borrow another group’s second set of cards or use an extra set to show sorting the cards in different ways to see multiple pattern possibilities.
Record with their group the patterns students noticed. Display slide M. After they have clarified their thinking, have students work with their group to write out how the patterns of body structures of their organisms are connected to either when or where they live(d) in the “How patterns of body structures are connected to my factor” section on their Patterns for My Organism:______________. They should individually list each relationship between their factor and the body structures of their organisms and number each one for reference in the next activity.
Universal Design for Learning: As a reminder, to support representation help students clarify the map symbols. On the maps, the blue color indicates water. The very light blue color indicates shallow seas or lakes. Deeper water is darker blue. Green or brown color indicates land. Green areas are covered with plants. Darker green indicates denser vegetation. Brown areas are drier with sparse vegetation. White areas indicate ice. During ice ages, the ice can cover large areas of land and water. Even in warmer climates, some areas, like Antarctica, may remain ice-covered.
While color coding is a useful way to quickly reference the parts of the map, letter or number coding helps ensure accessibility for any student who may be color blind. Consider adding additional coding to support your students as needed.

This is because the focus of this work is on working with ideas that other students shared in their arguments.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: Provide feedback regarding the presence or absence of the specific use of similarities and differences in body structures and the presence or absence of explicit reference to time and environments in the patterns they describe. Emphasize the role that students should adopt when they realize they missed a key point that a peer made in their arguments. In particular, remind students to ask their peers for clarification and/or restating of key ideas when they realize they have a gap in their recall or understanding of one or more of the ideas a peer shared.
Additional Lesson 5 Teacher Guidance
SUPPORTING STUDENTS IN MAKING CONNECTIONS IN ELA
CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.SL.8.1.D Acknowledge new information expressed by others, and, when warranted, qualify or justify their own views in light of the evidence presented.
On day 2 of this lesson, students have two opportunities to engage in respectful feedback conversations with their classmates:
as groups who examined similarities and differences in body structures of the same organism (horseshoe crabs, horses, or whales) come together and share their ideas and models
when students form triads to share their thinking and models showing relationships among body structures, time in which organisms live(d), and environments in which organisms live(d) for all three organisms investigated during this lesson
By this final unit of 8th grade, students should be very familiar with classroom norms that guide respectful conversations. Closely listening and trying to make sense of their peers’ ideas should be a well-established practice in small-group argument sharing. Students should be supporting their ideas and models with patterns in the data sets that their peers shared. Students should also be posing and responding to questions to elicit additional details or to clarify the patterns in these models when there is something they don’t understand.

assessments.title: Look for: environment changes or differences such as
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: environment changes or differences such as
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 6.B Ask questions related to what is causing changes in a whole population of organisms.
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for: Students should express ideas that include wondering about variation in a population, where new traits come from, and in particular, mechanisms related to how things change. Such mechanisms may include the following ideas:
environment changes or differences such as
climate
availability or distribution of food, water, shelter
type and number of predators
availability of mates
disease or absence of disease
something that happens within the individual in response to the environment
learning or experience resulting in acquiring new traits
changes in genes passed on (e.g., mutation) or inherited (recombination of genes through sexual reproduction)
something that time causes (e.g., long periods of time always lead to some change, change is constant)
something that is random
assessments.whatToDo: What to do: Use talk moves to lift ideas about how populations could be changing, such as asking another student to rephrase what they heard a classmate say. If students mention variation between individuals, ask them to clarify their statement about how that alone could be causing a population to change over time. If that leads them to realize they can’t explain it with variation alone, encourage them to write a question about it.

assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for
As students are completing their argument, circulate the room to check in to see if claims are aligned with the idea that penguins alive today descended from penguins that lived long ago and somehow the variations in their body structures have changed.
See Key: Argument for “How are penguins today connected to penguins from long ago?” for further scoring guidance.
What to do
If students are not using the idea that penguins had to come from somewhere, refer to the idea using different examples of animals coming from their parents. You could go back to the discussions in OpenSciEd Unit 8.5: Why are living things different from one another? (Muscles Unit) about cattle and even the planaria (we couldn’t have had two planaria if there wasn’t one before them to split).
If students are not bringing in the idea that the organisms must have changed over time, ask them to think about populations now and whether they are all the same with regard to every body structure and ask them to think about some of the body structures that show a lot of variation.
Universal Design for Learning: Allowing students to express their ideas using multiple modalities supports student ownership of their learning by giving students choice, access, and control in navigating their own understanding around the science ideas. Use this opportunity to encourage students’ action and expression by using different representations--symbols, colors, words, pictures. There will be moments throughout the unit where the class agrees on shared representations, but this is not necessary right now.

assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 6.A.2 Construct, use, and/or present an oral and written argument supported by empirical evidence and scientific reasoning to support an explanation for whether the types of things that lived long ago are ancestors to the modern organisms we see today (stability and change).
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for
During the Consensus Discussion for the ideas outlined in the Key Ideas box.
See Key: Argument for “How are penguins today connected to penguins from long ago?” for further scoring guidance.
What to do
If students are not using the idea that penguins had to come from somewhere, refer to the idea using different examples of animals coming from their parents. You could go back to the discussions in OpenSciEd Unit 8.5: Why are living things different from one another? (Muscles Unit) about cattle and even the planaria (we couldn’t have had two planaria if there wasn’t one before them to split).
If students are not bringing in the idea that the organisms must have changed over time, ask them to think about populations now and whether they are all the same with regard to every body structure and ask them to think about some of the body structures that show a lot of variation.
Add line of descendants to the Word Wall. A sample definition students might suggest is something like “organisms that can be traced directly to organisms in the past through parent-offspring relationships, for example, parents, grandparents, great-great-great-grandparents, all the way back through hundreds of generations”.
Motivate identifying the ideas we need to figure out to help us answer some big questions. Refer to the Penguin Timeline model and say, Let’s take a moment to put ideas together from what we are talking about now and what we figured out about the fossils representing populations. There must have been some populations of ancient organisms that had offspring that were lines of descendants that led to modern organisms.
As you say this, focus on one of the ancient penguin dots on the Penguin Timeline model.
Suggested prompt
Sample student response
Did we agree that this is just a single penguin, or does this dot represent at least a few penguins that were living at the same place and time?
The dot represents only the one or few fossils found, but there must have been more living at the same place and time because each penguin had to come from somewhere--it had to have parents. And each one likely had offspring.
So like over here (point and refer to a dot representing a generation of modern penguins and to the dot and arrow leading to it that represent the parental generation of penguins) where we showed that this generation of penguins each descended from a set of parents … do you think we could then draw the same dot and arrow back over here for each of these ancient penguins? Where would you put those?
Yes, those penguins must have also had parents, so you could draw a dot to the left of each dot and use an arrow to connect them like we did with the modern penguins.
(Draw a dot to the left of the ancient penguin dot and a right-pointing arrow in between, similar to how we did with modern penguins.) OK, so those penguins had parents, but do you think it is possible that those penguins also had offspring? If so, how could we represent them?
If the ancient penguins had offspring, we could show an arrow pointing from the fossil’s dot to a dot on the right.
(Draw an arrow leading from the ancient penguin’s fossil dot to a dot to the right.) OK, so earlier we wondered how far back these dots go (point to the modern penguin dots). How far forward do you think these dots would go? (Point to the fossil penguin dots.)
We’re not sure.
Maybe they connect to the modern penguins.
Maybe they just keep going and then stop if they went extinct.
Maybe they keep going but don’t connect to the modern penguins.
Even if these modern penguins don’t connect to these ancient penguins, what must be true? Do they connect to something?
Yes, they have to connect to something.
It could be the ancient penguins.
It could be some other organism.
It could be something we don’t have any fossil evidence for or something that looks so different we don’t know they would be connected.
Say, So even if we aren’t sure yet which lines of dots end up where,…

assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for
As you circulate among the groups while they work, listen for every student to participate. Conversations should refer to specific information about horseshoe crabs and/or specific parts of the General Model for Natural Selection.
Taken together, the written evidence on the sticky notes on the Small Group Working Copy of Our General Model should explain how and why the body structures of ancient horseshoe crabs have not changed much compared to modern horseshoe crabs.
All the elements in the model should be addressed.
Notes written on the model should refer to specific information from the reading or from their investigations in earlier lessons. General statements are not sufficient to explain this particular case.
The “Because of this . . .” statements should describe clear and accurate cause-and-effect relationships.
See Student Examples of Using General Model to Explain Body Structures for potential examples. Keep in mind that student language will vary from what is shown in the examples. Using specific information is important, but the precise words used in student explanations are not. Students who thoroughly understand and can apply the General Model for Natural Selection will provide a detailed set of statements containing all the elements specific for the body structure of horseshoe crabs they chose.
What to do
If students are struggling to participate, assign them a particular model element to identify and describe from the Reading v1: Horseshoe Crabs--Ancient and Modern reading. Point out if they have missed using an element in the model. Provide support but do not provide answers to specific student questions. Rather, redirect them to the resources they have available and remind them that they have done this kind of analysis before with different cases in this unit. Allow them to proceed independently.

assessments.title: Look for: What to look and listen for: Circulate among…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: What to look and listen for: Circulate among…
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 12.A.1 Construct a scientific explanation for how natural selection acting over generations has caused organisms’ body structures to change over time in response to changes in environmental conditions.
assessments.lookListenFor: What to look and listen for: Circulate among students as they talk with partners and listen closely as students share ideas with the whole class. Students should be actively engaged in connecting specific elements of the General Model for Natural Selection with specific information about ancient and modern horses, the environments they inhabited, and the functions of multiple and single toes. Listen for each student to make an accurate and specific connection between the model and the information about horses. An example of what specific information might be included is in Student Examples of Using General Model to Explain Body Structures. However, keep in mind that student language will vary from what is shown in the example. Using specific information is important, but the precise words used to describe connections are not.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students are struggling to make connections, point out one element of the model on their Progress Tracker Copy of Our General Model and ask them if any part of what they read connects with that element. Encourage them to look at one part at a time to see if it fits the general ideas. Or ask them what they found interesting about what they read and whether they can connect that with some part of the model. Celebrate accurate connections, even if they are tenuous, and encourage persistence.
It is always important that all students’ ideas are respected and taken seriously. Even though at this point in the unit there is a preponderance of evidence that supports the claim that natural selection is the mechanism underlying incremental changes in traits that can accumulate to produce large-scale structural changes, dissenting claims should be welcomed into the conversation.
However, it is also critical that scientific claims are always supported with evidence. The arguments supporting natural selection as the mechanism for change occurring over millions of years are solidly based in scientific evidence and reasoning and there is no evidence that contradicts them. The evidence cannot be based on direct observation since ancient organisms no longer exist and the fossil record is incomplete. Therefore, students may feel the support is weak. Ask students to explain the connection between their claims and the evidence that supports them.

assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for: Discussions and models should include the following ideas:
Species of penguins with the least number of differences on the data strips (and the most similarities) will have lived in the same environment together most recently and will share a more-recent common ancestor than species of penguins with more differences on the data strips.
Similarities and differences in body structures (on the data strips) are used as evidence to support the relationship between ancient and modern penguins. (Since there are a lot of missing data, there is more uncertainty in these explanations, so it is expected that these proposed relationships will vary greatly among groups.)
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: Remind students to use the sticky notes to record the number of differences they count between the species they are comparing. Body Structure Similarities and Differences between Modern Penguin Species is available for teachers to be able to quickly see if students are correctly assessing the number of differences in body structures between each of the species. However, if students have miscounted, don’t worry about correcting them; it is more important that they are using the ideas correctly and grouping the organisms based on the number of similarities and differences.
If students are struggling to participate, assign them a pair of species to analyze. Ask questions that require students to think about the patterns they are seeing in the data strips as they organize their Penguin Ancestry Model.

assessments.title: Look for: In the early phases of development, there are…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: In the early phases of development, there are…
assessments.buildingTowards: Building towards: 14.A.1 Analyze and interpret sketches of different species at different stages of embryological development to identify similarities and differences (patterns) in physical structures not evident in the fully formed anatomy.
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look and listen for: Listen for students to say something like the following:
In the early phases of development, there are many similarities in the structures of each of the organisms.
It is difficult to tell the organisms apart early in development, but by later in development their physical structures begin to look more different.
All the organisms early in development have a tail-like structure, an eye, an earhole or ear, and nubs where arms, fins, or legs will eventually develop.
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students struggle making comparisons between the different structures found in the embryo sketches, encourage them to think of an external structure that they know all the animals have, such as eyes. Then encourage them to look for evidence of this structure in the different sketches and color code it. Then prompt them to look for other common structures and color code if it is found in all or some of the embryo sketches. You will have a second opportunity to assess students in the following step.
Analyze and interpret the data with a partner. Display slide J. Say, Now work with a partner to compare what you both identified for the similarities and differences in the physical structures of the different animals. Record these in your notebook in the table you set up. You may wish to reproject slide H with the data table for students.
Give partners 8 minutes to compare their findings and fill in their data tables.
Bring the class back together. Display slide K and ask, What did you and your partner discuss?
Suggested prompt
Sample student response
What were some similarities you discovered in the physical structures of the organisms at different stages of development?
Note: Some examples are included here, but these are not exhaustive. Accept all student responses, encouraging them to explain the similarities specifically for each stage of development.
Early in development, all four looked very similar.
They each have a spot that looks like an eye and an ear hole.
They each have five little nubs, or bumps where arms and legs and the stomach grow.
They all have a tail.
The tail looks like it has ridges on it, like where the backbone will be?
Later in development, the fish and salamander look more similar to each other and the chicken and turtle look more similar to each other.
What were some differences you discovered in their physical structures at different stages of development?
Note: Some examples are included here, but these are not exhaustive. Accept all student responses, encouraging them to explain the differences specifically for each stage of development.
Later in the development, all four animals look different from each other.
By the time the animals are right before hatching, they all look very different from each other and more similar to adult animals.

assessments.title: Look for: Using productive talk strategies they have be…
assessments.shortTitle: Look for: Using productive talk strategies they have be…
assessments.lookListenFor:
What to look for and listen for: Focus on how students engage in the Scientists Circle discussion. Look for evidence of the following:
Using productive talk strategies they have been practicing all year
Respectfully providing and/or receiving critiques on scientific arguments by probing reasoning and evidence
Challenging ideas and conclusions (raising related questions)
Responding thoughtfully to diverse perspectives
Determining additional information required to resolve contradictions (and articulating the question this would help answer)
assessments.whatToDo:
What to do: If students are struggling to get the discussion started, remind them of the productive talk moves we have been using all year. In addition, refer them to the class norms, particularly the ideas about moving our science thinking forward and equitable representation (e.g., recruit neighbors to go public that we haven’t heard from).
Reflect on the progress made. Reserve 3 minutes at the end of this discussion to celebrate as a class. Emphasize how valuable it is to be still generating more questions and more ideas at this point in our work and how much this reflects the nature of science. Suggest that even though we appear on the cusp of being ready to form an entire new DQB, that this line of questions and ideas might be most productive to pursue in future years, such as in high school. Encourage students to keep marinating on these ideas and questions over the summer. Suggest that we return to our unit DQB next time to see if we can close up most if not all of our initial questions on it. Say, So let’s wrap up our DQB next time and really celebrate what we have figured out.
Collect New Ideas and Questions Connected to Embryo Comparisons.
Additional Lesson 14 Teacher Guidance
SUPPORTING STUDENTS IN MAKING CONNECTIONS IN ELA
CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.SL.8.1.C Pose questions that connect the ideas of several speakers and respond to others' questions and comments with relevant evidence, observations, and ideas.
CCSS.ELA-LITERACY.SL.8.1.D Acknowledge new information expressed by others, and, when warranted, qualify or justify their own views in light of the evidence presented.
At the end of this lesson, while they are in the Scientists Circle, students share and acknowledge new information expressed by others and, when warranted, qualify or justify their own views in light of the evidence presented. They also pose questions that connect the ideas of several speakers and respond to others' questions and comments with relevant evidence, observations, and ideas.

What to do:
If students struggle to provide the evidence and reasoning, give students examples and use questions to guide them. Ask them, How do you know that? What did we do in class that made you answer that way? How did that activity change your thinking?
If students need more challenges, ask them to connect their answers to the models or sketch the part of the model that their answer is about.
Review and share the questions that students think we have answered. Present slide B and have students mark on the class DQB with sticky dots the questions that they think we have made progress on.✱ Then have students move into their Scientists Circle.
Revisiting the DQB is important for students to feel as though their questions are valued and recognized. While not all questions will have been addressed (it’s more likely that 50-75 percent will be at least partially answered), this helps students see that they have done this hard work to answer many of their own questions.

assessments.whatToDo: What to do: If students struggle to answer questions from the DQB, place them in partners or small groups with one question or cluster of similar questions assigned to each group. Have them (1) locate where the questions most closely relate to the class’s consensus models from Lesson 4 (Penguin Timeline with Cards) or Lesson 8 (General Model for Natural Selection) and then (2) examine their science notebook and other documents to search for evidence that could answer or partially answer the question. Ask the group to co-construct, in writing or orally, an explanation to the question(s) using evidence from their previous work. Remind students what makes a good explanation is a how or why causal account that can be supported with evidence.
